title: Pushes and pulls
source: DeepKids Combined. Covers Cambridge Stage 1 Physics (pushes and pulls, toys, changing movement). No textbook needed.
summary: Everything that moves was pushed or pulled. Your child finds pushes and pulls in the playground, in toys and at home, discovers that a bigger push makes things go faster and further, and that a push or pull can also slow things down, stop them or turn them.
builds_on: This is the first time. Later classes come back to forces: shapes changing (Class 2), measuring forces and friction (Class 3), spinning and floating (Class 4), and air, water and many forces at once (Class 5).
goals: By the end your child can show a push and a pull with their body and with objects, and say which one they used.
By the end your child can explain that things do not start moving by themselves: something has to push or pull them.
By the end your child can show that a bigger push makes a ball or car go faster and further.
By the end your child can use a push or pull to speed something up, slow it down, stop it and change its direction.
By the end your child can predict before testing, and say whether the guess was right.
words: to press something away from you
to go from one place to another
the way something is going: left, right, up, down
to guess what will happen before you try it

days.title: Push or pull?
days.goal: Notice that we move things by pushing and pulling them.

steps.title: Move the chair
steps.do: Put a light plastic chair in the middle of the room. Ask your child: 'Can you make the chair come to you without walking to it?' Let them try (they may ask you, or tie a dupatta to it). Then ask: 'Now make it go far away from you.' Say: 'When you made it come to you, that was a pull. When you made it go away, that was a push.'

steps.title: Simon says push, Simon says pull
steps.do: Play Simon Says with actions. 'Simon says push a door', 'Simon says pull a drawer', 'Simon says pull up your socks', 'Simon says push a button', 'kick a ball' (no Simon: they freeze). After each action ask: 'Push or pull?' Kicking is a push. Opening a fridge door is a pull. Pressing the lift button is a push. If they are unsure, ask: 'Did it go away from you or come towards you?'

steps.title: Push and pull hunt
steps.do: Walk around the home together with Worksheet ws1 (Push or pull?). At each thing, your child does the action and you both decide: tap (push), drawer (pull), switch (push), zip (pull), kneading atta (push), rolling a roti with a belan (push), ringing a cycle bell (push), pulling a curtain (pull). Some things need both: a swing, a broom, a door. Say: 'Some jobs need a push AND a pull. Which ones did we find?'

steps.title: Show me with your hands
steps.do: Say 'push' and 'pull' in a random order, faster and faster. Your child shows each with their hands: palms pushing away, or fists pulling in. Then ask: 'What is a push or a pull called by scientists?' Answer: a force. Let them say the word three times in a funny voice.

days.title: Playground forces
days.goal: Find pushes and pulls on swings, slides, see-saws and balls.

steps.title: Park scientists
steps.do: Go to a park or open space. At the swing ask: 'How does the swing start moving? What makes it go higher?' (Someone pushes it; pushing at the right time makes it go higher.) At the slide: 'Who pushes you down the slide?' (Nobody! The Earth pulls you down. That pull is called gravity, they will learn more about it later.) At the see-saw: 'How do you make your side go up?' (Push the ground with your feet.) Play catch: 'Did I push or pull the ball to throw it? Did you push or pull to catch it?' (Throwing is a push; catching is a pull towards you and then a push to stop it.)

steps.title: Tug of war
steps.do: Play tug of war with a dupatta, two or three people if you can. Ask: 'Are we pushing or pulling?' (Pulling.) 'Why did the rope move towards the winner?' (Their pull was bigger.) Then try pushing palm to palm with your child, gently. Ask: 'When nobody moves, are we still pushing?' (Yes, both pushes are equal, so nothing moves.)

steps.title: Draw one
steps.do: At home, your child draws one thing from the park and an arrow showing the push or pull. Show them how: the arrow points the way the force goes. Write 'push' or 'pull' next to it for them if they cannot write yet. Then ask the question in voice v2: 'When you throw a ball, your hand lets go. So what keeps it flying?' Listen to their idea first, then tell them what Ibn Sina thought.

days.title: How toys work
days.goal: Discover that every moving toy needs a push or pull to get going.

steps.title: Toy parade
steps.do: Your child brings five toys that can move: a car, a ball, a top (lattu), a pull-along toy, a yo-yo, a spring toy, a doll's pram. Ask about each: 'How do we make it move?'

steps.title: Sort the toys
steps.do: Make two places on the floor with paper labels 'push' and 'pull'. Your child plays with each toy and puts it on the right label. A car pushed along goes on 'push'. A pull-along toy goes on 'pull'. A lattu: you pull the string, so 'pull'. A yo-yo needs both: put it in the middle. Ask: 'Did any toy start moving all by itself?' (No. Even a wind-up toy needed you to turn the key first, which pushes a spring tight inside.)

steps.title: Play the Push and Pull board game
steps.do: Print the game (Game: Push-Pull Path) and play it with a coin as the counter and a die. On each square your child does the action and says push or pull before moving on. It's fine to land on squares more than once; they get faster each time.

days.title: Big push, small push
days.goal: Find out that a bigger push makes things go faster and further.

steps.title: Gentle or strong?
steps.do: Roll a ball to your child very gently, then a bit harder. Ask: 'Which one came faster? What did I do differently?' (A bigger push.)

steps.title: Ramp race
steps.do: Do Experiment e1. Your child predicts first, then tests. Measure how far the car goes with steps (heel to toe) or with a string, and put a sticky note where it stops each time.

steps.title: What does it mean?
steps.do: Look at the sticky notes. Ask: 'When did the car go furthest? Why?' Good answer: 'When the ramp was higher, the car got a bigger push from the slope and went faster.' Then ask: 'Was your guess right? Is it OK if a guess is wrong?' Say: 'Scientists make wrong guesses all the time. Testing is how they find out.'

need: a flat board or big book for a ramp

days.title: Slow down, stop, turn
days.goal: Use pushes and pulls to slow things down, stop them and change their direction.

steps.title: Stop the ball
steps.do: Roll a ball towards your child. Ask them to stop it with a hand, then a foot, then a cushion. Ask: 'What did you do to stop it?' (Pushed against it.) 'Which was the softest stop?' (The cushion.)

steps.title: Ball goal
steps.do: Make a goal with two slippers. You roll the ball slowly across the room, and your child has to change its direction with one tap so it goes into the goal. Then try speeding it up with a tap, and slowing it down. After each, ask: 'Did your push speed it up, slow it down, stop it or turn it?'

steps.title: Which floor slows it most?
steps.do: Do Experiment e2. Roll the same car with the same push (let it go from the same ramp) onto three floors: tiles, a durrie or carpet, and a towel. Mark where it stops.

steps.title: Why did it stop?
steps.do: Ask: 'Nobody touched the car. Why did it stop on the towel?' Accept: 'the towel was bumpy', 'the towel held it back'. Say: 'The rough towel rubs against the wheels and pulls them back. Scientists call that rubbing force friction. We'll find out much more about it in Class 3.'

need: a toy car and ramp from Day 4
a towel and a durrie or carpet

days.title: Teach it back
days.goal: Show what you know about pushes and pulls, and talk about the big questions.

steps.title: Make it move
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws2 (Make it move) together. Read each question aloud; your child answers by pointing, drawing or saying.

steps.title: A big question
steps.do: Ask the big question: 'What pushes the wind?' and 'Who pulls a ripe mango down from the tree?' There's no wrong answer; listen and ask 'how could we find out?' Then talk about voice v1: long ago, a famous thinker said things stop moving because stopping is natural. Galileo tested it and found that things only stop because something slows them down. Ask: 'Our car stopped on the towel. Was that natural, or did something slow it?'

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child is the teacher and you are the student who knows nothing. Ask them the check questions in a confused voice ('How do I open the fridge? Do I push it?') and let them explain and show. Finish by asking them to show you one push and one pull that we did not find this week. If they enjoyed this, try the puzzles on Worksheet ws3 together another day.

sections.p: Find one thing at home that needs a push AND a pull. Draw it.
Which push makes the car go furthest?
A ball is rolling. You tap its side. What happens?
Which floor stops a rolling car fastest?
What did the push or pull do?
Draw a toy and an arrow showing the push or pull that makes it move.
A ball is lying still on the floor. Can it start rolling all by itself? Why or why not?
You and your friend push a box from opposite sides with the same push. What happens? Why?
What pulls you down a slide?

experiments.title: Ramp race
experiments.question: Does a higher ramp make the car go further?
need: a flat board or big hardback book
books to build the ramp up
steps: Lean the board on one book to make a low ramp.
Let the car go from the top. Do not push it, just let go.
Put a sticky note where the car stops.
Add a second book to make the ramp higher. Let the car go again and mark it.
Add a third book and try again.
experiments.predict: Ask your child to guess first: 'Which ramp will make the car go furthest: low, middle or high?' Write the guess down.
experiments.observe: Where the car stops each time. Measure with steps or string.
experiments.why: On a higher ramp, the Earth's pull has longer to speed the car up as it comes down, so the car reaches the floor going faster and rolls further before the floor slows it down.

experiments.title: Which floor slows it most?
experiments.question: Which floor makes a rolling car stop soonest?
need: the ramp from e1 (two books high)
steps: Put the end of the ramp on the tiles. Let the car go and mark where it stops.
Lay the towel at the end of the ramp. Let the car go from the same place and mark it.
Do the same with the durrie or carpet.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Which floor will stop the car quickest?'
experiments.observe: How far the car rolls on each floor.
experiments.why: Rough surfaces rub against the wheels more. That rubbing (friction) pulls back on the car and slows it down sooner. On smooth tiles there is less rubbing, so it rolls further.

activities.title: Tug of war and palm push
steps: Hold opposite ends of the dupatta and pull gently.
Let your child win once by pulling harder.
Then push palm to palm with the same strength so nobody moves.
Ask what happened in each case.
activities.outcome: Your child feels that a bigger pull wins, and that equal pushes cancel out.

project.title: Make a push-pull toy
steps: Choose a toy to make: a matchbox car pulled by a string, a paper ball you blow with a straw, or a 'spinning' bottle cap.
Make it from things at home: a matchbox, bottle caps for wheels, string, a straw.
Test it: how do you make it go? Push or pull?
Make it go further. What did you change?
Show it to the family and explain the push or pull.
project.outcome: A home-made toy and a short show-and-tell.

game.title: Push-Pull Path
rules: Do the action on your square and say 'push' or 'pull'. Get it right: stay. Wrong: go back 1.
Squares with a star let you roll again.
squares: Slide down: who pulls you? Back 1
Car on a towel: slow down, miss a turn

big: Why does a mango fall down from the tree and not up?
Could anything ever start moving all by itself?
Is a magnet pushing or pulling when it grabs a pin?

challenge.q: People used to think things stop moving because stopping is natural. Is that true? What made our car stop?
challenge.hint: Try the car on tiles and on a towel. If stopping were natural, would the floor matter?

challenge.q: We say 'the wind pushed the door shut'. Can air push? How could you show it without touching the door?
challenge.hint: Blow through a straw at a paper ball, or wave a newspaper at a feather.

perspectives.view: Pulling a cart is easier on a smooth road than on a muddy field. Ask: why would mud make the bullocks work harder?
In kabaddi, a raider is pulled back by the whole team. One pull against many. Ask: who wins and why?
An ant can carry many times its own weight by pushing against the ground with six legs. Ask: if you were as strong as an ant for your size, what could you lift? Who is really the strong one?

voices.who: Aristotle (384–322 BCE), Greece, and Galileo Galilei (1564–1642), Italy
voices.idea: Aristotle taught that the natural state of things is to be still, so a moving thing stops on its own unless something keeps pushing it.
voices.then: For almost 2,000 years most people agreed. Galileo rolled balls down ramps and onto smooth surfaces and saw that the smoother the surface, the further the ball rolled. He argued that a ball on a perfectly smooth, flat surface would keep rolling for ever.
voices.now: Galileo was right, and Isaac Newton later made it the first law of motion. Things only slow down because something, like rubbing or air, pushes back on them.
voices.ask: Our car went further on the tiles than on the towel. Which idea does that agree with, Aristotle's or Galileo's?

voices.idea: Ibn Sina disagreed with Aristotle's idea that the air keeps pushing a thrown stone along. He said the thrower gives the stone an inner 'inclination' (mayl) to keep moving, which is used up as the air and the ground resist it.
voices.then: Later thinkers in Europe, like Jean Buridan in the 1300s, developed a similar idea they called 'impetus'. It was a big step away from Aristotle.
voices.now: Today we say a moving thing keeps moving by itself unless a force slows it; nothing inside it gets used up. Ibn Sina was right that the air is not what keeps it going, and right that resistance slows it down.
voices.ask: Is a thrown ball carrying something inside it that runs out, or does it just keep going until something slows it? How could you test it?

books.title: Forces Make Things Move
books.author: Kimberly Brubaker Bradley
books.why: A clear picture book about pushes, pulls and why things move.

books.title: Rosie Revere, Engineer
books.author: Andrea Beaty
books.why: A girl builds machines that fail, and learns that failing is how you get better.

books.title: The Most Magnificent Thing

check.q: Show me a push and a pull.
check.a: Any correct action: pushing a door, pulling a drawer.

check.q: What is another name for a push or a pull?
Can a ball start rolling all by itself?
check.a: No, something has to push or pull it.

check.q: How do you make the car go further?
check.a: Give it a bigger push, or use a higher ramp.

check.q: How can a push or pull change how something moves?
check.a: It can speed it up, slow it down, stop it or change its direction.

check.q: Why did the car stop sooner on the towel?
check.a: The rough towel rubbed on the wheels and slowed it down.

story.title: Tara and the Wall That Pushed Back
text: The rain had been falling on Tara's chawl in Mumbai for three whole days, and Tara was cross. She was cross with the rain for keeping her indoors. She was cross with the grey sky. But most of all she was cross with her baby brother, Chintu, who had been born in the summer and had been the centre of everything ever since.
"Everyone looks at Chintu," she said to nobody. "Chintu sneezed. Chintu smiled. Chintu did a burp." She stamped to the door of their room. "I don't need anyone. I'm going to push everything away."

She put both hands flat on the wooden door and pushed it shut. Bang. That felt good. But something strange happened as she pushed: she felt the door pushing her hands back. She took her hands away and looked at them. Pink, a bit squashed. She pushed the door again, gently this time, and there it was: the door was pressing back on her palms, exactly as hard as she pressed it.

She went to the wall, the thick old wall that had stood since before her Aaji was born, and she pushed it as hard as she could. She pushed until her face went red and her elbows shook. The wall did not move at all. But her hands hurt, and her feet slid backwards on the floor.
"Aaji," she called, "the wall is pushing me!"

Aaji was sitting on the mat, folding clothes, with Chintu asleep beside her like a small warm loaf. She did not laugh. She put down the shirt she was folding. "Of course it is," she said. "Nothing in the whole world can be pushed without pushing back. Not doors. Not walls. Not even the floor under your feet. When you walk, you push the floor behind you, and the floor pushes you forward. That is the only reason you can walk at all."

Tara thought about this. She walked across the room very slowly, feeling each foot press down and back, and the floor quietly pressing her up and on. She had walked ten thousand times and never once said thank you to the floor.

The next day the rain stopped. The courtyard was shining, and the older children brought out their roller skates. Tara's cousin Imran lent her his old pair, and Chintu, who could now sit up, was placed in a cardboard box on wheels that Imran had made, and everyone took turns pulling him around.

When it was Tara's turn, she was still a little bit cross. She stood behind Chintu's box on her skates and gave it a big push to send it away from her. Whoosh, off went the box across the wet stone. But Tara went whooshing too, backwards, the other way, her arms flapping, until she bumped into the water tank and sat down with a splash.

Everyone laughed, and so, after a moment, did Tara. But as she sat there in the puddle, she understood something she could not quite put into words. When she pushed Chintu away, she had been pushed away too. You could not do one without the other.

She got up. She skated carefully to the box, where Chintu was waving his fat hands at her. She held out her hands, and he grabbed her fingers with his tight baby grip. And then Tara pulled. Gently. And as she pulled him towards her, she rolled towards him, and they met in the middle of the courtyard, the box and the girl, and spun round once, slowly, together.
Aaji was watching from the balcony. She did not say anything. She just smiled and went back inside to fold the clothes.
story.epiphany: Newton's third law, felt in the body at age 6: every push or pull is a pair. You can't push without being pushed back, and when you pull something to you, you move towards it too. The story's turn is Tara sliding backwards when she pushes Chintu away. It also quietly says that we are never separate from what we touch.
ask: When Tara pushed the door, what did she feel? Try it now with a door.
Why did Tara roll backwards when she pushed Chintu's box?
When you walk, what pushes you forward?
What happened when she pulled instead of pushed?
Can you think of anything you can push that doesn't push you back?

ideas.idea: You can't push anything without being pushed back.
ideas.more: Push a wall and feel your hands squash. Stand on a skateboard or in socks on a smooth floor and push a friend: you both move apart. Scientists call this Newton's third law; you can feel it long before you can name it.

ideas.idea: Nothing starts, stops or turns by itself.
ideas.more: A ball on the floor stays there for ever until something pushes it. A rolling ball would roll for ever if nothing slowed it down. That was Galileo's great idea.

ideas.idea: We walk, swim and fly by pushing the world.
ideas.more: Feet push the floor back; fish push water back; birds push air down. Everything that moves itself does it by pushing something else.

unknowns: Why does a moving thing keep moving if nothing stops it? Scientists can describe it perfectly, but why the universe works this way, nobody knows.
What is the pull that brings a mango down from the tree? We call it gravity, and we can measure it very precisely, but what gravity really is is still one of the biggest mysteries in science.
